title: The Pivotal Moments That Gave Rise to Silicon Valley - Semiwiki
gist: Historical essay by Sunil Mehta (posted by SemiWiki Admin, promoting his novel The Compass) arguing Silicon Valley's rise was contingent, with Robert Noyce at most pivotal junctures. Most investor-relevant is Noyce's 1964-65 below-cost, $1 IC anticipatory pricing, which Gordon Moore called as important as the IC itself.

insights.claim: In 1964 Fairchild sold some low-end ICs below manufacturing cost, betting that lower prices would raise demand, volume would improve yields and lower costs, and falling costs would spur more demand.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Classic learning-curve pricing playbook still relevant to evaluating aggressive pricing in new chip categories.
insights.locator: In 1964, he made a startling decision

insights.claim: In 1965 Noyce announced Fairchild would price its major IC products at one dollar apiece, a strategy Gordon Moore later called an 'invention' as important to the industry as the integrated circuit itself.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Pricing ahead of the cost curve can create the volume that makes it profitable.

insights.claim: Noyce pitched Sherman Fairchild that silicon and metal were cheap raw materials, so competition would lie in the ingenuity and manufacturing technology used to transform them.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Early articulation of manufacturing know-how as the semiconductor moat.

insights.claim: The author argues Silicon Valley's rise was not inevitable but a succession of chance encounters and risky decisions, with Robert Noyce present at an extraordinary number of pivotal moments.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Narrative history; limited direct investment relevance.

insights.claim: Arthur Rock's 1957 idea to build a company around engineers rather than place them in an established firm was rejected by dozens of corporate backers before Sherman Fairchild agreed, founding Fairchild Semiconductor.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Origin of the venture-backed startup model.

insights.claim: Noyce's planar-process-based monolithic IC, with metal interconnects on oxide and p-n junction isolation, scaled where Texas Instruments' Kilby 'solid circuit' with external flying wires could not, solving the 'tyranny of numbers'.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Manufacturability, not first invention, determined the winning architecture.
insights.locator: Noyce’s concept had been developed independently

insights.claim: Fairchild delivered 100 transistors to IBM five months after founding despite not having built one when it accepted the order, using two parallel development efforts.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Parallel bets to de-risk development, an enduring execution tactic.
insights.locator: Noyce organized two parallel development efforts

insights.claim: In the early 1960s Noyce sent Julius Blank and Charlie Sporck to Hong Kong, leading Fairchild to set up a major assembly operation there, an early milestone in semiconductor globalization.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Roots of today's Asia-centric back-end supply chain.

insights.claim: Intel returned Busicom's $60,000 development investment in exchange for rights to sell the 4004 processor beyond calculators, announced November 15, 1971.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Securing IP rights cheaply enabled the microprocessor business.

insights.claim: By end of 1971 Intel's 1103 DRAM was the world's largest-selling semiconductor device, and with the 4004 and 1702 EPROM Intel had all three building blocks of digital electronics.
insights.speaker: Admin
insights.so_what: Historical context for Intel's founding franchise.
insights.locator: 1971: The Year the Pieces Came Together
